messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 64

He is a 41-year-old Middle Eastern man who works in fast food and lives alone, though he speaks often of family members who live nearby and remain a steady presence in his life. When he first begins to describe what happened, he does so carefully, as if he is still deciding whether the story can be told all the way through. The event itself is not something that happened to him directly, but something he witnessed while working late one night at a restaurant with a drive-through window. A young man in the parking lot is struck during a violent altercation outside the store, and the scene unfolds too quickly for anyone to stop it. He remembers the sound first—the shouting, a crash, then a body hitting the ground—and he remembers standing frozen behind the counter with his hands still full, unable to move toward the door or away from it. In the days afterward, he keeps replaying the moment in fragments, returning again and again to the one detail he believes he should have changed if he had reacted faster.

Before the incident, he describes himself as steady and private, someone who keeps his head down, works hard, and takes pride in being reliable. He has spent years in food service, mostly in late shifts and fast-paced kitchens where the work is repetitive but manageable. After the trauma, that familiarity changes. He continues to show up for work, but he becomes more alert than before, scanning the parking lot whenever headlights sweep across the windows or an argument rises near the counter. He finds himself listening for changes in tone, watching hands, watching doors. He says he cannot stop his body from preparing for danger even when nothing is happening. At night, he checks locks several times before he can sleep, then lies awake feeling his chest tighten as he imagines the scene returning in the dark.

His memories of the event come back without warning. Sometimes they arrive when he is cutting vegetables, hearing a sudden clatter in the kitchen, or when a customer raises his voice over a missing order. In those moments he feels as though he is back in the parking lot again, staring at the same terrible scene and trying to make sense of it. He does not describe these experiences dramatically; instead, he speaks about them with a tired disbelief, as if he is still embarrassed by how completely his mind and body react. He avoids driving by the restaurant when he is off work, and he has begun taking longer routes home to stay away from the place where it happened. He declines invitations from friends to go out at night, saying he is too tired, though it is clear that what he is really trying to avoid is the feeling of being trapped in another sudden emergency.

He notices that his moods are flatter than before. He used to joke with coworkers and call his sister every few days, but now he answers briefly and often says he is fine when he is not. He feels detached from other people, especially from coworkers who did not see the event and seem able to move on. At times he becomes irritable over small things, snapping at a colleague for leaving the prep area messy or feeling angry when customers complain about delays. He is ashamed of this anger and keeps it mostly inside, but it leaks out in tension in his jaw, in restless pacing during breaks, in the way he grips the steering wheel too hard on the drive home. He says he no longer feels like the same easygoing person he was before. There is a sadness in him that he has trouble naming, a sense that something has been broken open and never properly closed.

He also struggles with sleep. He falls asleep late, wakes often, and sometimes wakes from dreams with his heart pounding, not always remembering the content but knowing it is connected to what he saw. Because of this, his mornings begin already exhausted. He relies heavily on caffeine to get through long shifts, then feels more keyed up and less able to settle. He has started missing small details at work, forgetting orders or needing reminders from coworkers, and this frustrates him because he prides himself on being dependable. Even on quieter days, his body feels tense, as if waiting for the next explosion of noise. He says he has not felt truly safe since that night.

Over time, he begins to understand that the event has changed the shape of his ordinary life. The restaurant is still open, the grill still hisses, the fryers still bubble, but he experiences each shift against a background of danger. He continues to work because he needs the income and because routine helps him stay afloat, yet he does so with a constant inward vigilance that leaves him drained. He presents as someone trying hard to remain functional while carrying a memory that will not stay in the past.
